## Objectives

+ Produce an **exponential smoothing** forecast and explain what the smoothing
  factor $\alpha$ does.
+ Produce an **exponential smoothing with trend adjustment** forecast and
  explain what $\beta$ does.
+ **Tune** $\alpha$ and $\beta$ on the data, and say why a parameter tuned on
  the whole sample is not the same as one that would have worked in real time.
+ Recognise when a smoothing method is being beaten by a trend, and fix it.

::: {.charcoal}
Before Exam 1 you built forecasts by averaging the last few values. Two things
were wrong with that, and you saw both on the CPI. A moving average forgets
everything older than its window, and it remembers everything inside the
window equally. Exponential smoothing fixes both with one parameter: it
remembers *everything*, but with weights that shrink geometrically into the
past. Then the trend-adjusted version fixes the lag you watched every average
suffer on a rising series.

You have been submitting challenge forecasts for six weeks now. Bring your
backtest tables. By the end of this note you should know whether to switch
methods, and be able to say why in two sentences.
:::

# Exponential Smoothing

::: {.blue}
**Exponential smoothing** adjusts the previous forecast by a fraction of the
previous period's forecasting error (Formula 16.2):

$$F_t = F_{t-1} + \alpha\,(A_{t-1} - F_{t-1}),$$

where $F_t$ is the forecast for period $t$, $A_{t-1}$ the actual value in
period $t-1$, and $\alpha$ the **smoothing factor**, $0 \le \alpha \le 1$.
:::

Read the formula as a sentence: *next forecast = last forecast, corrected by
a share of how wrong it was.* If last quarter's forecast was too low (positive
error), the new forecast goes up; too high, it comes down. Donnelly calls it
"self-correcting". The size of the correction is $\alpha$.

::: {.charcoal}
Do not confuse this $\alpha$ with the $\alpha$ of a hypothesis test. Same
letter, no relation. Forecasters and hypothesis testers both got there first.
:::

## Priming the pump

To forecast period 13 you need the forecast for period 12, which needs the
forecast for period 11, and so on back to period 1 — which has no earlier
period. The convention is to set $F_1 = A_1$ and start. That first "forecast"
was assigned, not calculated, so it gets no forecasting error and it is left
*out* of the MAD. Leaving it in would hand the method a free zero and make
the comparison with the moving averages unfair.

With Brandywine Ford's sales and $\alpha = 0.6$:

```{python}
#| label: es-math
#| output: asis
a = CAR_SALES.values
F2 = a[0] + 0.6 * (a[0] - a[0])
F3 = F2 + 0.6 * (a[1] - F2)
F4 = F3 + 0.6 * (a[2] - F3)
show_math(r"\begin{aligned} F_1 &= A_1 = %d \\ F_2 &= F_1 + 0.6\,(A_1 - F_1) = %d + 0.6\,(%d - %d) = %.1f \\ F_3 &= F_2 + 0.6\,(A_2 - F_2) = %.1f + 0.6\,(%d - %.1f) = %.1f \\ F_4 &= F_3 + 0.6\,(A_3 - F_3) = %.1f + 0.6\,(%d - %.1f) = %.1f \end{aligned}"
          % (a[0], a[0], a[0], a[0], F2, F2, a[1], F2, F3, F3, a[2], F3, F4))
```

Notice $F_4$: the period-3 error was $108 - 124 = -16$, so the forecast came
*down* by $0.6 \times 16 = 9.6$. That is the self-correction.

```{python}
#| label: es-table
es6 = exp_smooth(CAR_SALES, alpha=0.6)
error_table(CAR_SALES, es6).round(1)[["actual", "forecast", "error", "abs_error"]]
```

The forecast for 2019Q1 is `{python} num(es6.iloc[-1])` cars and the MAD is
`{python} num(mad(CAR_SALES, es6))` — averaged over eleven errors, periods 2
through 12. That is *worse* than every moving average from Part 1. Donnelly's
point, and it bears repeating: no method wins on every series. With this
$\alpha$ on this series, exponential smoothing loses.

## What $\alpha$ does

A large $\alpha$ carries most of the last error forward: the forecast chases
the data and jumps around. A small $\alpha$ barely reacts: the forecast is
smooth and slow. The role is the same as the window length $p$ in a moving
average, and the right value depends on the data in the same way.

```{python}
#| label: es-alpha-plot
_ = forecast_plot(CAR_SALES, {"alpha = 0.2": exp_smooth(CAR_SALES, 0.2),
                              "alpha = 0.8": exp_smooth(CAR_SALES, 0.8)},
                  title="Figure 16.6: the effect of alpha on the forecast", ylab="Cars sold")
```

Why "exponential"? Unwind the formula once: $F_t = \alpha A_{t-1} + (1-\alpha) F_{t-1}$.
Unwind it again and $F_{t-1}$ contains $\alpha A_{t-2}$ weighted by
$(1-\alpha)$; unwind again and $A_{t-3}$ carries $(1-\alpha)^2$. Every past
value is in the forecast, with weights $\alpha, \alpha(1-\alpha),
\alpha(1-\alpha)^2, \ldots$ — a weighted moving average over the *whole*
history, with weights that decay exponentially. With $\alpha = 0.6$ the value
from four periods ago has weight `{python} num(0.6 * 0.4**3, 3)`. With
$\alpha = 0.1$ it still has weight `{python} num(0.1 * 0.9**3, 3)`.

## Tuning $\alpha$

Since $\alpha$ is a choice, choose it the way you chose $p$: compute the MAD
for a range of values and look.

```{python}
#| label: es-curve
curve = tune_alpha(CAR_SALES, grid=np.round(np.arange(0.05, 1.0, 0.05), 2))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.2))
ax.plot(curve.index, curve["MAD"], color=UNLV_SCARLET, marker="o", linewidth=1.4)
ax.set_xlabel("alpha"); ax.set_ylabel("MAD")
ax.set_title("Figure 16.5: the MAD is U-shaped in alpha", color=UNLV_SCARLET)
ax.grid(axis="y", color="#e6e6e6")
for side in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

The MAD is smallest at $\alpha$ = `{python} num(curve["MAD"].idxmin(), 2)`,
where it is `{python} num(curve["MAD"].min())` — the book eyeballs "around
0.35". Even at its best, exponential smoothing does not catch the four-period
moving average on this series (`{python} num(mad(CAR_SALES, sma_forecast(CAR_SALES, 4)))`).
The seasonal pattern is the reason, and nothing in this note fixes it; that
is Part 3.

::: {.scarlet}
A tuned parameter is a *description of the past*. The $\alpha$ that minimises
the MAD over 2022–2026 is the one that would have done best *if you had known
it in 2022*, which you did not. Below we check whether a tuned $\alpha$ still
wins when it is chosen only from data available at the time. When it does not,
the tuning has fitted noise. This is the single most useful habit you can take
from this course into any job that involves a model.
:::

## Excel, for the record

Excel's Data Analysis tool asks for a **damping factor**, not $\alpha$. The
damping factor is $1 - \alpha$: enter 0.4 to get $\alpha = 0.6$. The output
column is offset by one row and begins with `#N/A` — that is period 1 having
no forecast, which is correct. If you ask Claude to build the workbook, say
"damping factor 0.4" and check that the first numeric cell is 97.

# Exponential Smoothing with Trend Adjustment

Every method so far lags a trending series, because every one of them
forecasts from a level and a trend keeps moving the level. The fix is to
smooth two things: the level, and the *change* in the level.

::: {.blue}
**Exponential smoothing with trend adjustment** (Formulas 16.3–16.5):

$$\begin{aligned}
F_t &= \text{FIT}_{t-1} + \alpha\,(A_{t-1} - \text{FIT}_{t-1}) && \text{the smoothed level} \\
T_t &= \beta\,(F_t - F_{t-1}) + (1-\beta)\,T_{t-1} && \text{the smoothed trend} \\
\text{FIT}_t &= F_t + T_t && \text{the forecast including trend}
\end{aligned}$$

with $\beta$, the trend smoothing factor, also between 0 and 1. Start with
$F_1 = A_1$, $T_1 = 0$.
:::

$T_t$ is a weighted average of the *most recent* change in the level
($F_t - F_{t-1}$, weighted $\beta$) and the *accumulated* trend so far
($T_{t-1}$, weighted $1-\beta$). A large $\beta$ believes the latest change; a
small $\beta$ believes the long-run drift. Then the forecast is the level plus
one period's worth of trend.

With $\alpha = 0.3$ and $\beta = 0.1$ (Table 16.6):

```{python}
#| label: est-table
est = exp_smooth_trend(CAR_SALES, alpha=0.3, beta=0.1)
tbl = est.round(1)
tbl.insert(0, "actual", list(CAR_SALES.values) + [np.nan])
tbl["abs_error"] = error_table(CAR_SALES, est)["abs_error"].round(1).reindex(tbl.index)
tbl
```

Follow one row. For period 3: the level $F_3 = 97.0 + 0.3(142 - 97.0) = 110.5$;
the trend $T_3 = 0.1(110.5 - 97.0) + 0.9(0) = 1.4$; the forecast
$\text{FIT}_3 = 111.9$. The last row is the forecast for 2019Q1:
`{python} num(est["FIT"].iloc[-1])` cars, MAD `{python} num(mad(CAR_SALES, est))`.
Better than plain exponential smoothing at $\alpha = 0.6$, still not better
than the four-period average. The trend is real but small (about 2.5 cars a
quarter), and the seasonal swings are ten times larger.

```{python}
#| label: summary-cars
pd.set_option("display.float_format", lambda v: f"{v:,.1f}")
accuracy(CAR_SALES, {
    "naive": naive_forecast(CAR_SALES),
    "SMA p=3": sma_forecast(CAR_SALES, 3),
    "SMA p=4": sma_forecast(CAR_SALES, 4),
    "WMA 3-2-1": wma_forecast(CAR_SALES, [1, 2, 3]),
    "ES alpha=0.6": es6,
    "ES+trend 0.3, 0.1": est,
}).round(1)
```

This is Donnelly's Table 16.7, with the naive row added and two extra
yardsticks. Read it as the book does: choose the four-period SMA, and do not
conclude that simple always beats sophisticated. It depends on the series, and
now we go to the series that matter.

# The Challenge Series

## The CPI: tune, then check the tuning

```{python}
#| label: cpi-curves
pd.set_option("display.float_format", lambda v: f"{v:,.3f}")
cpi_curve = tune_alpha(cpi)
cl_curve = tune_alpha(claims)
a_cpi, a_cl = cpi_curve["MAD"].idxmin(), cl_curve["MAD"].idxmin()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))
for ax, (c, title) in zip(axes, [(cpi_curve, "CPI"), (cl_curve, "Weekly claims")]):
    ax.plot(c.index, c["MAD"], color=UNLV_SCARLET, marker="o", linewidth=1.3)
    ax.set_title(f"{title}: MAD by alpha", color=UNLV_SCARLET)
    ax.set_xlabel("alpha"); ax.grid(axis="y", color="#e6e6e6")
    for side in ("top", "right"):
        ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Two very different curves. The CPI wants the largest $\alpha$ we tried
(`{python} num(a_cpi, 2)`): a trending series wants to chase the level, and
the more it chases, the closer it gets to the naive forecast. Claims settle at
$\alpha$ = `{python} num(a_cl, 2)`: noisy and flat, so some averaging helps,
but not much. The parameter is describing the series.

Now the trend component. A grid over $\alpha$ and $\beta$ for the CPI:

```{python}
#| label: cpi-grid
grid = tune_alpha_beta(cpi, alphas=np.round(np.arange(0.1, 1.0, 0.2), 1),
                       betas=np.round(np.arange(0.1, 1.0, 0.2), 1))
best = grid.stack().idxmin()
grid.round(3)
```

Smallest MAD at $\alpha$ = `{python} str(best[0])`, $\beta$ = `{python} str(best[1])`:
`{python} num(grid.loc[best], 3)`, against `{python} num(mad(cpi, naive_forecast(cpi)), 3)`
for the naive forecast that won Part 1. A method knows, for the first time,
that the CPI drifts upward, and that is what "same as last month" could never
know.

```{python}
#| label: cpi-summary
next_month = (cpi.index[-1] + pd.offsets.MonthBegin(1)).strftime("%B %Y")
cpi_methods = {
    "naive":                              naive_forecast(cpi),
    "SMA p=3":                            sma_forecast(cpi, 3),
    f"ES alpha={a_cpi:.2f}":              exp_smooth(cpi, a_cpi),
    f"ES+trend {best[0]}, {best[1]}":     exp_smooth_trend(cpi, best[0], best[1]),
}
accuracy(cpi, cpi_methods).round(3)
```

That is the whole-sample verdict for `{python} next_month`. Here is the one
that counts — the last 24 months replayed one at a time, each forecast made
with only the data that existed then:

```{python}
#| label: cpi-backtest
bt = backtest_summary(cpi, {
    "naive":            (naive_forecast, {}),
    "SMA p=3":          (sma_forecast, {"p": 3}),
    "ES 0.5":           (exp_smooth, {"alpha": 0.5}),
    f"ES {a_cpi:.2f}":  (exp_smooth, {"alpha": a_cpi}),
    "ES+trend 0.5, 0.3": (exp_smooth_trend, {"alpha": 0.5, "beta": 0.3}),
    f"ES+trend {best[0]}, {best[1]}": (exp_smooth_trend, {"alpha": best[0], "beta": best[1]}),
}, last=24)
bt.round(3)
```

Winner: **`{python} bt["MAD"].idxmin()`**, with a backtested MAD of
`{python} num(bt["MAD"].min(), 3)` index points against
`{python} num(bt.loc["naive", "MAD"], 3)` for naive. The tuned parameters
survived the backtest, which is the evidence you need before submitting them.
Notice also that an *untuned* trend-adjusted model ($0.5, 0.3$) beats naive
too: the gain is from modelling the trend at all, not from the fine tuning.

```{python}
#| label: cpi-plot
_ = forecast_plot(cpi, {"naive": cpi_methods["naive"],
                        f"ES+trend {best[0]}, {best[1]}": cpi_methods[f"ES+trend {best[0]}, {best[1]}"]},
                  title="CPI: the trend-adjusted forecast stops lagging", ylab="Index", last=24)
```

## Weekly claims: no trend to adjust

```{python}
#| label: claims-backtest
pd.set_option("display.float_format", lambda v: f"{v:,.1f}")
btc = backtest_summary(claims, {
    "naive":            (naive_forecast, {}),
    "SMA p=2":          (sma_forecast, {"p": 2}),
    "SMA p=4":          (sma_forecast, {"p": 4}),
    f"ES {a_cl:.2f}":   (exp_smooth, {"alpha": a_cl}),
    "ES+trend 0.3, 0.1": (exp_smooth_trend, {"alpha": 0.3, "beta": 0.1}),
}, last=26)
btc.round(1)
```

Over the last 26 weeks the best is **`{python} btc["MAD"].idxmin()`**. The
trend-adjusted model, which rescued the CPI, sits at
`{python} num(btc.loc["ES+trend 0.3, 0.1", "MAD"], 0)` here — it is
estimating a trend that does not exist and paying for the noise it picks up
doing so. A component you model that is not there costs accuracy, exactly as
one you fail to model does.

## Nevada house prices: quarterly, trending, and turning

```{python}
#| label: hpi-setup
pd.set_option("display.float_format", lambda v: f"{v:,.2f}")
recent = hpi.loc["2015Q1":]
hc = tune_alpha(recent)
a_h = hc["MAD"].idxmin()
hpi_methods = {
    "naive":               naive_forecast(recent),
    "SMA p=2":             sma_forecast(recent, 2),
    f"ES {a_h:.2f}":       exp_smooth(recent, a_h),
    "ES+trend 0.5, 0.3":   exp_smooth_trend(recent, 0.5, 0.3),
    "ES+trend 0.9, 0.1":   exp_smooth_trend(recent, 0.9, 0.1),
}
accuracy(recent, hpi_methods).round(2)
```

```{python}
#| label: hpi-backtest
bth = backtest_summary(recent, {
    "naive":             (naive_forecast, {}),
    "SMA p=2":           (sma_forecast, {"p": 2}),
    f"ES {a_h:.2f}":     (exp_smooth, {"alpha": a_h}),
    "ES+trend 0.5, 0.3": (exp_smooth_trend, {"alpha": 0.5, "beta": 0.3}),
    "ES+trend 0.9, 0.1": (exp_smooth_trend, {"alpha": 0.9, "beta": 0.1}),
}, last=8)
bth.round(2)
```

```{python}
#| label: hpi-plot
_ = forecast_plot(recent, {"naive": hpi_methods["naive"],
                           "ES+trend 0.9, 0.1": hpi_methods["ES+trend 0.9, 0.1"]},
                  title="Nevada house price index: actual vs. forecast",
                  ylab="Index, 1980Q1 = 100", last=24)
```

```{python}
#| label: hpi-winners
#| include: false
ws_win = accuracy(recent, hpi_methods)["MAD"].idxmin()
bt_win = bth["MAD"].idxmin()
```

The whole-sample winner is **`{python} ws_win`**; the backtest winner is
**`{python} bt_win`**. When those two differ, the disagreement is
information: the index rose steeply through 2022 and has flattened since, so
a model tuned on eleven years has learned the steep part while a model judged
on the last eight quarters is being asked about the flat part. A series that
has changed character rewards the method closest to now, and the backtest is
the one to believe.

::: {.charcoal}
This is the quarterly series in the challenge. You get two forecasts of it
all semester, so there is no learning from mistakes in real time. Everything
you know has to come from the backtest.
:::

## Verify

| Check | What it catches |
|---|---|
| The first forecast equals the first actual ($F_1 = A_1$) | A different priming rule, which changes every number after it |
| The MAD counts $n-1$ errors, not $n$ | Period 1's free zero being counted |
| Excel's damping factor is $1-\alpha$, not $\alpha$ | The single most common Excel mistake in this chapter |
| The tuned $\alpha$ was chosen on a stated grid | "Optimal" from a tool you cannot see |
| The backtest winner is the one you are submitting | A whole-sample winner that fell apart in real time |
| A tiny $\beta$ with a large $\alpha$ is nearly naive — say so if that is what won | Sophistication that is doing no work |

the senior-fall GPA with exponential smoothing, $\alpha = 0.4$, and its MAD;
(b) repeat with trend adjustment, $\alpha = 0.5$, $\beta = 0.7$. By hand first.

say by how much, over how many periods, and on which series it would have
been a mistake.
